newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasury, Wal-Mart discuss Cuban pajamas.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasury, Wal-Mart discuss Cuban pajamas.

text.p: Lawyers for retailing giant Wal-Mart Stores Inc. were talking with the U.S. Treasury Department about a cross-border tug-of-war over whether Wal-Mart may sell Cuban-made pajamas in Canada, a Treasury official said on Friday.

The Canadian government has pressured Wal-Mart Canada into putting the cotton pajamas back on store shelves, placing the retailer in potential breach of U.S. laws aimed at bringing economic pressure against the Cuban government headed by Fidel Castro.
Treasury, which is in charge of enforcing an embargo against any U.S.-owned company's trade with Cuba, appeared determined to ensure that American law was obeyed.
"Our interest is in enforcing the embargo," said Howard Schloss, Treasury's assistant secretary for public affairs.
"We've had discussions and we will have more discussions with Wal-Mart on this and that's about where we are right now," Schloss said.
Attempts to reach representatives of Wal-Mart at its Bentonville, Ark., headquarters were unsuccessful.

Wal-Mart's Canadian unit pulled the pajamas from the shelves on February 27 but on March 4, Canadian Trade Minister Art Eggleton announced an investigation into whether Wal-Mart had violated Canada's Foreign Extraterritorial Measures Act.
Yesterday Wal-Mart Canada said it had decided to resume selling the C$12.96 (US$9.53) pajamas, one of about 80,000 items its Canadian subsidiary markets.

Canada, with a 10th of the population of its powerful Southern neighbor, is acutely sensitive to any threat to its sovereignty. Its extraterritorial measures law provides for fines up to $1.5 million Canadian dollars against violators.
The battle over Wal-Mart sales in Canada of Cuban pajamas occurs against a broader background of Canadian, European and Mexican anger about a year-old U.S. measure known as the Helms-Burton law.

That law, signed into law by President Clinton after Cuban MiG fighters shot down two small private U.S. planes off Cuba in February 1996, seeks to compel other nations to join U.S. efforts to isolate Cuba.

Named after its Republican sponsors, Jesse Helms and Dan Burton, the law codified Washington's 35-year embargo on Cuba and included an additional provision to punish some foreign firms doing business with Cuba.

The law would allow Americans to file lawsuits in U.S. courts against foreigners considered to have benefited from property confiscated by the Cuban government since Castro's communist regime seized power in 1959. However, Clinton has so far waived this portion of the law.
On Friday, the State Department stepped up pressure against Canada by barring four more executives of Canadian mining concern Sherritt International from entering the United States.

Sherritt was previously sanctioned under Title IV of Helms-Burton, by which senior executives of foreign firms deemed to be "trafficking" in property confiscated by Castro's 1959 revolution may be barred entry to the United States.
Sherritt has vowed to stay on in Cuba.

Canada never joined the embargo against Cuba nor prevented its citizens from traveling to Cuba. Popular Cuban products like rum and Havana cigars are readily available in Canada and Cuba is a favored destination for sun-seeking Canadian tourists.
